pages.name: The power scrubber
pages.text: The heater test's 10 Ω element on a 100 V peak, so its current peaks at 100 ÷ 10 = 10 A. The voltage and the dashed current top out together: they are [[in phase]]. Below is the [[instantaneous power]], volts × amps as on DC, at each instant. Drag the time cursor and watch the dot ride it.
pages.alt: 10 Ω element, 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 5.0 ms the voltage is 100.0 V and the current 10.00 A, so the power then is 1000 W. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle.

pages.name: At the bottom
pages.task: The cursor is parked at 15 ms, the bottom of the cycle: −100 V and −10 A. What power does the element take at that instant?
pages.why: The power at an instant is that instant's voltage × its current: −100 × −10 = +1000 W, because a minus times a minus is a plus. The element heats whichever way the current flows, just as at the top of the wave. The power is zero only where both waves cross zero, at 0, 10 and 20 ms.
pages.alt: 10 Ω element, 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 15.0 ms the voltage is −100.0 V and the current −10.00 A, so the power then is 1000 W. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle.

pages.name: Two humps a cycle
pages.text: Now the cursor sweeps one whole cycle, 20 ms, leaving a trace. While the voltage is forward the power rises to 1000 W and falls back: one hump, 10 ms long. While it is backward both readings are negative, and a minus times a minus is a plus: a second hump, just the same. So the power pulses at double the supply's frequency, two humps a cycle, 100 a second on 50 Hz.
pages.alt: 10 Ω element, 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 20.0 ms the voltage is 0.0 V and the current 0.00 A, so the power then is 0 W. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle.

pages.name: On board ship
pages.task: 60 Hz is the most common frequency on board ship. How many power humps a second does this element give there?
pages.why: Every cycle has a forward half and a backward half, and each gives a hump: 2 humps a cycle × 60 cycles a second = 120 humps a second. 60 would be one hump a cycle, as if the backward half gave nothing. 240 doubles twice.
pages.alt: 10 Ω element, 100 V peak, 60 Hz. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle.

pages.name: The average
pages.text: So how much heat does the element give on average? Its power is 100 sin × 10 sin = 1000 sin², 1000 W × the sine squared. Remember Calculus fundamentals' fold: the top of each hump fits exactly into the dip beside it, so the humps average half their top, 500 W, the [[average power]]. The rms values give it straight away: each is 0.707 of its peak, and 70.7 V × 7.07 A is about 500 W, because 0.707 is 1 ÷ √2, and 1 ÷ √2 squared is a half.
pages.alt: 10 Ω element, 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 5.0 ms the voltage is 100.0 V and the current 10.00 A, so the power then is 1000 W. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle, averaging 500 W.

pages.name: Averaging first
pages.task: Over a whole cycle the voltage averages 0 V and the current 0 A. What power does the element average?
pages.why: It is the product that has to be averaged, and the product never goes below zero: humps from 0 to 1000 W, averaging half their top, 500 W, which is 70.7 V × 7.07 A. Averaging the voltage and the current first lets each backward half cancel its forward half, but in the product the backward half heats the element just as well, because a minus times a minus is a plus. 1000 W is only the top of each hump, for an instant.
pages.alt: 10 Ω element, 100 V peak, 50 Hz. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle, averaging 500 W.

pages.name: A mains heater
pages.text: Now the mains card: a 1 kW heater on 230 V mains is 230² ÷ 1000 = 52.9 Ω, drawing 230 ÷ 52.9 = 4.35 A. Its voltage peaks at 325 V and its current at 4.35 × √2 = 6.15 A. The dashed average sits at 230 V × 4.35 A = 1000 W, and the humps reach twice that, 2000 W, about 325 × 6.15, for an instant each.
pages.alt: 1 kW heater, 52.9 Ω, on 230 V mains. At 5.0 ms the voltage is 325.3 V and the current 6.15 A, so the power then is 2000 W. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle, averaging 1000 W.

pages.name: The clamp meter
pages.task: A clamp meter reads 10 A on a heater at 230 V. What is its average power, and how high do its humps reach?
pages.why: The clamp meter shows an rms value (lesson 2), and the 230 V is rms too, so multiply them: 230 V × 10 A = 2300 W, the average. The humps top out at twice that, 4600 W, for an instant each: the peaks, about 325 V × 14.1 A. Taking 4600 W as the average puts the heat at the tops; halving 2300 W halves once too often, because the rms values already allow for the humps.
pages.alt: a clamp meter reads 10 A on a 230 V heater. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle, averaging 2300 W.

pages.name: A faster supply
pages.text: Watch the supply switch to 60 Hz, the most common frequency on board ship. The humps crowd closer, 120 a second, but their tops stay at 1000 W and the average at 500 W, because a resistor's current follows its voltage at each instant, whatever the frequency. Now switch back and forth between 50 Hz and 60 Hz, and drag the cursor.
pages.alt: 10 Ω element, 100 V peak, 60 Hz. At 5.0 ms the voltage is 95.1 V and the current 9.51 A, so the power then is 905 W. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle, averaging 500 W.

pages.name: From the tops
pages.task: A heater's power humps top out at 3000 W. What is its average power?
pages.why: For a sine, the tops of the humps fit into their dips, so the humps average half their top: 3000 ÷ 2 = 1500 W. 3000 W is reached only for an instant. 2120 W uses 0.707 once on the power, but 0.707 belongs to the voltage and to the current; the power takes it twice, and 0.707 × 0.707 is a half.
pages.alt: a heater's power humps, tops at 3000 W. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle, averaging 1500 W.

pages.name: Mixed: the shape of the power
pages.task: Mixed. Which is true of the 10 Ω element's power?
pages.answer: It reaches zero twice each cycle and never goes below it
pages.why: The power is the voltage × the current. Both cross zero together twice a cycle, so the power touches zero there. On the backward half both are negative, so their product is positive. 500 W is its average, not a steady value: it swings between 0 and 1000 W.
pages.alt: 10 Ω element, 100 V peak, 50 Hz. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle.

pages.name: Mixed: a ship heater
pages.task: Mixed. A heater element across 440 V at 60 Hz draws 10 A. What is its power?
pages.why: Rms volts × rms amps: 440 × 10 = 4400 W, 4.4 kW, in humps that come twice a cycle, 2 × 60 = 120 a second. The peaks, about 622 V and 14.1 A, multiply to 8.8 kW, the top of each hump, twice the heat. 60 a second would be one hump a cycle.
pages.alt: a heater on 440 V at 60 Hz, drawing 10 A. The power wave stays at or above zero, two humps a cycle, averaging 4.4 kW.
